Inserting a template:

1. Copies the module into the project's `graphics/` folder under a free name
   (a second Lower third becomes `lower-third-2`, and so on). The two then
   show under This Project as "Lower third — lower-third" and "Lower third —
   lower-third-2".
2. Places one graphic clip at the playhead, on the front track if it fits
   there, otherwise on a new track above everything. With a nest open, the
   clip goes on the nest's front track, or a new track inside the nest.
3. Selects the new clip so the inspector shows its Graphic sub-tab.

Inserting a graphic from **This Project** places a clip drawn by that module
as it is, the same way, and copies nothing.

**From File…** names the module after the chosen file: the name is
lowercased, each run of characters other than a–z and 0–9 becomes one `-`,
dashes are trimmed from the ends, the result is cut to 60 characters, and an
empty result becomes `graphic` (so `My Title.js` becomes `my-title`). If that
name is taken, it gets `-2`, `-3` and so on.

On the timeline a graphic clip is labelled **Graphic**, with a `{}` glyph, and
has no filmstrip.

The clip's length and size come from the module's own `meta`
(`durationInFrames`, `width`, `height`) when it gives them; otherwise it is
5 seconds long and the canvas's size. A graphic is placed at Fit scale, like a
shape.

Placing the clip is one undo step, **Insert Graphic**. Copying the file into
the project is not undone. If the module doesn't compile, no clip is placed:
the dialog stays open with the first error and its line under the lists (for
From File…, an alert says it); a template's copy stays in `graphics/`. A file
that isn't UTF-8 text is refused.

Insert ▸ Graphic… is greyed until the project's window is open.

*Agents:* `list_graphics` lists what the dialog shows, and `insert_graphic`
(`name`, `from`: `template` or `project`) is its Insert; or `write_graphic`
then `add_graphic_clip` (`track`, `at`, `name`, and optionally `duration`,
`width`, `height`, `props`).

### Sharing a graphic
model needs your own key for it, and without the key the command is greyed
rather than hidden:

- **Your AssemblyAI key** (Transcription, below) turns on the AssemblyAI
  engine of **File ▸ Generate Captions…** and the **Transcribe** buttons of
  **Clip ▸ Remove Filler Words…**. With no key, **Generate** is greyed when
  the AssemblyAI engine is chosen (unless every file is already transcribed,
  see [Captions](captions.md)), each **Transcribe** button is greyed, and
  **Clip ▸ Remove Filler Words…** itself is greyed and reads **Remove Filler
  Words… (needs your AssemblyAI key)** — unless a file in the project already
  has a transcript made with filler words, which it keeps using without a
  key.
- **Your Anthropic key** (Assistant, below) turns on the assistant. With no
  key, **View ▸ Assistant** still opens the Assistant tab, which says how to
  add the key.

Resting the pointer on a greyed control shows "No AssemblyAI API key is set.
Set one in Frame Job ▸ Settings… ▸ Transcription." (or the same sentence for
Anthropic and **Assistant**). Saving the key turns the commands on at once,
even with the sheet still open; there is nothing to relaunch. Everything that
runs on your Mac — on-device captions, Remove Silences, Enhance Voice and the
rest — needs no key.

Settings is one window, not a set of tabs. It holds four sections, top to
bottom: **MCP**, **Assistant**, **Transcription** and **Playback**. On a
short screen the window stops at the screen's height and scrolls. Closing it
loses nothing: every control saves as you use it, or when you press its
**Save** button, as described below. While it is open it is listed in the
**Window** menu, so you can bring it back from behind other windows.

The Assistant, Transcription and Playback headings each carry an ⓘ button.
Rest the pointer on it for a moment to see that section's explanation; click
it to keep the explanation open, and click it again (or anywhere else, or
press Escape) to close it.

## Where audio lives

There is only one kind of track. Any track can hold a clip with sound, whether it is a video file, an audio-only file (a voice-over, music, a recorder

The waveform shows the level of the file itself, so moving the Volume slider doesn't redraw it. It's drawn faded when the clip is muted, when its trac

When the selection includes at least one clip that plays sound, the Clip tab of the inspector shows a **Sound** sub-tab. A clip counts as having sound

1. **Volume**: level, gain read-out, loudness read-out, Mute, Normalize and Enhance Voice
2. **Fades**: fade in and fade out
3. **Ducking**: lowers every other clip while this one plays
4. **Voice Isolation**
5. **Voice Effect**: one of sixteen effects, from a pitch shift to a cathedral
6. **Channels**: which channels of a stereo file play
7. **EQ**: a high-pass, two shelves, three bands and a low-pass, with presets for voice
8. **Hum**: removes mains hum and its harmonics
9. **Noise Reduction**
10. **Gate**: turns the pauses between phrases down
11. **Leveller**: evens out a speaker who moves on and off the mic
12. **De-esser**: tames harsh "s" sounds
13. **Compressor**
14. **Mix**: pan, mix to mono, Detach Audio and Attach Audio
15. **Limiter**: holds the clip's peaks under a ceiling

Voice Isolation through Limiter appear in the order the sound passes through them. Volume, the fades and ducking are applied last, like a fader.

Every section header has a summary and a Reset button that appears when the section differs from its default. The summaries read:

| Section | Summary |
|---|---|
| Volume | "muted", "silent" (at 0 %), or the gain, for example "+3.5 dB" |
| Fades | both lengths, for example "0.50 · 1.00 s", or "none" |
| Ducking | the duck level, for example "20%", or "off" |
| Voice Isolation | the amount, for example "80%", or "off" |
| Voice Effect | the effect and its amount, for example "Space: Hall 100%", or "off" |
| Channels | "Both", "Left Only", "Right Only" or "Swap Left and Right" |
| EQ | how many parts are on, for example "2 on", "bypassed", or "off" |
| Hum | the mains and the harmonics, for example "60 Hz · 4", or "off" |
| Noise Reduction | the amount, for example "50%", or "off" |
| Gate | the threshold, for example "−10 dB", or "off" |
| Leveller | the target, for example "0 dB", or "off" |
| De-esser | the frequency, for example "6.0 kHz", or "off" |
| Compressor | the ratio, for example "3.0:1", or "off" |
| Mix | "centre", "mono", or the pan position, for example "left 40" |
| Limiter | the ceiling, for example "−1.0 dBTP", or "off" |

 When you change a control with several clips selected, the change goes to all of them. A control whose clips hold different values is marked mixed.

| **Background** | The colour behind every layer. Lower its opacity for a transparent background; the section's note then names the export formats that keep transparency, or counts them when there are three or more. | Black, opaque |
| **Timecode** | Frames (`HH:MM:SS:FF`) or Milliseconds (`HH:MM:SS.mmm`), everywhere the project shows a time. | Frames |
| **Fit new clips to canvas** | A clip added from a file larger than the canvas is scaled down to fit. | On |

**Reset** on the section header puts all three back to their defaults. It is offered only while one of them differs.

### Markers

Every marker in the project, with its name, **Chapter**, **Go** and **Delete**. See [Timeline](timeline.md).

*Agents:* `set_canvas` (takes `width`, `height`, `fps`, `background`, `rescale_clips`, `fit_new_clips`, `timecode_frames`, `output`, `blending`; anything left out keeps its value; `fps` takes any `[num, den]`).

----
### Animated colours

When an action changes a colour (the text colour, its outline or backdrop, a
word-caption colour, the drop shadow or the chroma key colour), the colour
blends through the OKLab colour space. This avoids the muddy midpoint a
straight RGB blend gives. See [Motion and transitions](motion-and-transitions.md).

Shape colours (stroke, fill and gradient stops) cannot be animated: a
shape's styling always changes the clip itself, even while an action is
selected.

----
### Camera layouts

A screen recording with a camera in front of it can switch between layouts as
it plays. Put the playhead where the switch should happen and choose one from
**Clip ▸ Camera Layout ▸**:

- **Corner ▸**, **Rounded Corner ▸** and **Circle ▸**, each with **Bottom
  Right**, **Bottom Left**, **Top Right** and **Top Left** — the camera in a
  box a quarter of the canvas wide and a third tall, 5 % in from the edges, as
  a recording lands it. Corner shows the whole camera picture with square
  corners, Rounded Corner rounds them, and Circle crops the largest square of
  the picture to a circle. The screen fills the canvas as Add Clip places it.
- **Side by Side** — the screen fitted in the left two-thirds, the camera
  cropped to fill the right third, with a margin around and between them and
  slightly rounded corners.
- **Stacked** — the screen across the top, the camera cropped to fill the rest
  below it.
- **Camera Full** — the camera fills the canvas.
- **Screen Only** — the camera is hidden where it is (its opacity goes to 0),
  and the screen fills the canvas.

**Which clips:** with two clips with a picture selected on different tracks,
the front one is the camera and the other the screen. With one selected, it is
the camera and the screen is the clip drawing behind it at the playhead (the
front-most one on a shown track that is not a matte track). With none
selected, the camera is the clip at the playhead on the front-most track named
"Camera" — the track a recording's camera lands on. The item is greyed when
there is no such camera at the playhead, or a sheet is open. It works inside
an open nest too. Side by Side and Stacked need a screen; the other three lay
out a camera alone.

**The switch** eases over half a second from the playhead — a layout action on
each clip, which you see on its action lane and can retime like any other. At
a clip's first frame it cuts instead: the layout becomes the clip's own
placement there. Choosing another layout while one is still easing ends the
first where the second begins. One **Undo** takes the whole switch back.

**How far it reaches:** a layout holds until the next switch. Every later clip
on the camera's track (and on the screen's) that starts before the next layout
action on that track takes the layout as its own placement — so a camera cut
into pieces stays in the corner — and keeps its own actions.

**The Layout section:** with one video clip selected, the Clip tab's Picture
sub-tab has a **Layout** section (after Transform and Behind Subject, shut
until you open it): **Layout** (Corner, Side by Side, Stacked, Camera Full,
Screen Only), **Shape** (Square, Rounded, Circle) and **Corner** (Bottom Right,
Bottom Left, Top Right, Top Left) — Shape and Corner only for Corner — a
**Duration** for the switch (0.5 s to start, 0.01–10 s) and **Switch at
Playhead**, which does exactly what the menu does with this clip as the camera
and the clip behind it as the screen. The section's choices stay while the
window is open and are not saved; there is no Reset. Pressed with the playhead
off the clip, the inspector's foot says the clip does not play there and
nothing changes.

**Centred on the person:** Circle, Side by Side and Stacked crop the camera.
When the camera clip's person masks are already made for every frame it plays
— Remove Background makes them, and they stay in the project's cache — the crop
centres on the person (the middle of where the masks find them, averaged over
the clip) instead of on the middle of the picture. A layout never starts that
analysis itself: with no masks, or masks for only part of the clip, the crop
centres on the picture.

**Zooms:** a switch never fights a zoom. When a clip it would move holds a zoom
(or another action that moves it) after the playhead, the switch is refused.
A screen that is still at its full placement is not asked in Corner, Camera
Full and Screen Only, because those leave it where it is and its zooms keep
playing. When nesting those clips would let the switch go ahead, a sheet asks
**Lay out the clips in a nest?**, with the reason it was refused: **Nest and
Switch** puts the clips in a nest first, so the layout moves the nest and the
zooms keep playing inside it — the nest and the layout are one **Undo** —
and **Cancel** changes nothing. Otherwise the inspector's foot names the clip
and the action. A nest clip shows square corners only, so Rounded Corner and
Circle are refused on a nest clip camera.

*Agents:* `switch_layout {camera, screen?, layout, shape?, corner?, at,
duration?, curve?, focus?, nest?, through?}` — `focus` centres the camera's
crop on a point of its picture; left out, it is filled from the camera clip's
person masks as the menu fills it, and the answer's `focus` says what was sent
(null for none). It is never filled when `nest: true` nests the camera itself.
An agent is never offered the sheet: it sends `nest: true` to nest in the same
step. `through` stops the layout holding at a time.

**In a vertical version:** **File ▸ Make Vertical Version…** keeps the camera
layouts: each switch is made again on the new canvas at the same time, length
and curve, Side by Side becoming Stacked on a tall canvas, and the camera and
screen are never followed (see
[Vertical and framing](vertical-and-framing.md#make-vertical-version)). A
layout whose camera or screen was moved by hand after the switch is kept as
placed and named in the summary. *Agents:* `reframe_clip {follow: "layout",
from_width, from_height}` on the camera does the same for one camera.

### Hide while silent
----
### The Text tab

| Section | Rows |
|---|---|
| **Content** | A multi-line text area. Return, Tab or a click away applies it and gives the keys back to the editor; ⇧Return, ⌘Return, ⌥Return or ⌃Return starts a new line |
| **Font** | **Family** (every font installed on the Mac, plus the faces the app ships with: Source Sans 3, Source Serif 4, Montserrat, Anton, Bebas Neue, Darker Grotesque and IBM Plex Mono), **Style** (that family's faces), **Size** 6–800 px |
| **Style** | **Color**, **Align** (L / C / R), **Vertical** (top / middle / bottom within the box), **UPPERCASE**, **Line spacing** 0.5–4× (default 1), **Tracking** −20 to 100 px (default 0) |
| **Outline** | **Outline** on/off, **Width** 0–40 px (default 2), **Color** (default black) |
| **Backdrop** | A plate behind the text: **Backdrop** on/off, **Fill** (default black at 60 %), **Padding** 0–200 px (default 12), **Radius** 0–200 px (default 8) |
| **Box** | **Mode**: **Auto-size** (the box fits the words) or **Fixed width** (the words wrap). **Width** is 20–20000 px, starting at 60 % of the canvas width |
| **Reveal** | How the text arrives and leaves: **None**, **Typewriter**, **Word Fade** or **Line Rise**, with separate **In** and **Out** durations (0–10 s; In defaults to 1 s and Out to 0) measured from the clip's first and last frame |
| **Presets** | One-click looks, described below |

UPPERCASE changes only how the text is drawn: what you typed is kept as typed.
A text clip also gets the Picture tab's Transform, Shadow, Filters,
Reflection, Spotlight and Obscure sections.

Every frame of a reveal is worked out by the same calculation for the
preview, a rendered frame and an export, so the three always agree. A text
clip made by word captions has a word style, and while it does, the Reveal
section is greyed with "Word style wins; the reveal does not apply." (see
[Captions](captions.md)).

import sys,collections,json,math
sys.argv=['x']
import build as b
tax=b.build()
pages=[(s,p) for s in tax['sections'] for p in s['pages']]
import glob
recs=[]
for f in sorted(glob.glob(b.RAW+'/*.json')): recs+=json.load(open(f))
docs=[];df=collections.Counter()
for s,p in pages:
    t={b.stem(x) for x in b.toks(p['title']+' '+p['slug'].split('/')[1].replace('-',' '))}
    bd={b.stem(x) for x in b.toks(p['scope'])}
    docs.append((t,bd))
    for x in t|bd: df[x]+=1
n=len(pages); idf=lambda t:math.log(1+n/(1+df[t]))
area={a:s['id'] for s in tax['sections'] for a in s['areas']}
names=collections.defaultdict(set)
for r in recs:
    q={b.stem(x) for x in b.toks(r['name'])}
    best=(0,None)
    for (s,p),(t,bd) in zip(pages,docs):
        sc=sum(2*idf(x) if x in t else idf(x) if x in bd else 0 for x in q)
        if area.get(r['area'])==s['id']: sc*=1.5
        if sc>best[0]: best=(sc,p['slug'])
    names[best[1]].add(r['name'].lower())
rank=sorted(((len(v),k) for k,v in names.items() if k),reverse=True)
print('TOP',rank[:45])
print('LOW',[x for x in rank if x[0]<=3])
json.dump({k:sorted(v) for k,v in names.items() if k},open('assign.json','w'),indent=0,ensure_ascii=False)
E

content.content:
### Loop

Turn on **Loop** in the toolbar to loop playback. With an in/out range set it
loops the range; otherwise it loops the whole timeline. Pressing play at or
past the end of the loop starts again from the loop's start. Loop is set per
window and isn't saved.

---
### Speed

The **Speed** row sits under Format (under Dynamic Range in an HDR project). It is live only on **AV1 (MP4)** and **AV1 (WebM)**; on every other format it is greyed out and keeps your last choice. **VP9 (WebM)** and **VP

| Choice | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Faster** | The quickest AV1 export and the largest file. On 10 seconds of 4K camera footage it took about half Balanced's time (7.1 s against 14.0 s on an Apple M2 Max) and wrote a file 27 % larger; at 1080p 2.4 s ag
| **Balanced** | The default. |
| **Smaller file** | The slowest AV1 export and the smallest file. On the same footage it took about 1.4 times Balanced's time (19.9 s against 14.0 s at 4K, 5.8 s against 4.2 s at 1080p) and wrote a file 12 % smaller at 

AV1 and VP9 are encoded in software, so they take longer than the HEVC formats, which use the Mac's hardware encoder. The choice is remembered with the rest of the sheet and stored in presets.

---
### Bit depth

The **Bit depth** row sits under Quality. It is live only on **Audio only (WAV)** and **Audio only (AIFF)**; on every other format it is greyed out and keeps your last choice. **16-bit** is the default; **24-bit** keeps detail 16-bit cannot, which matters most for a quiet recording you are going to raise or process later. Both are rounded once from the mix, never dithered. ProRes's sound stays 16-bit. The choice is remembered with the rest of the sheet and stored in presets.

---
## What an export includes

- **The same picture and sound as the preview.** The export uses the same composition and the same compositor. View-only settings never reach it: Preview Quality, Show Ungraded, Show SDR Version, Show
- **Speed ramps and Keep pitch off.** An export waits for the rendered audio of every speed ramp, and of every clip at a constant speed other than ×1 with Keep pitch off, to finish before it writes, a
- **Remove Background.** A clip with Remove Background is drawn as the person alone in every frame of the file. Its person masks are made on this Mac as soon as the cutout is set, and an export waits,
- **The gate, the leveller and the de-esser.** Their thresholds follow each clip's measured loudness, and the leveller works from the clip's speech too, so an export waits, showing "Preparing…", until
- **Missing media.** A clip whose file is missing still exports, showing its slate and with no sound. An audio track none of whose clips can be read is written as silence instead of failing the export
- **Graphics.** An export draws the graphics as they were when it was asked for, even if a module is saved again mid-export. If a graphic in the range, or in a nest the range reaches, does not compile
- **Captions** are ordinary text clips, so they are always burned into the picture. To write a separate subtitle file, use **File ▸ Export Captions…** (see [Captions](captions.md)).

---
## Chapters

Chapter markers on the timeline (see [Timeline](timeline.md)) become chapters in MP4, MOV, M4A and WebM files, in time order. A chapter's name is the marker's name, or "Chapter *n*" for an unnamed one. A range export kee

MP4 and M4A files are written with their index at the front, so a player can start before the whole file has downloaded.

---
### A window

Choose **Window…** in **Source** and macOS's window picker opens. Click the window you want. The Source row then reads **Window (picked)** and the recording is that window alone, at its own size. If you cancel the picker

When **Include Frame Job windows** is off, the picker lists none of Frame Job's windows. When it's on, the picker lists them, but never the recorder panel. The box only changes the next time the picker opens. A window yo

If you press Record while the row reads **Window…** with nothing picked, the panel says "Choose a window with Window… first, or pick a display." and nothing records.

---
### The menu-bar item

While a recording runs, Frame Job puts an item in the menu bar: a coral **●** and the elapsed time (`m:ss`, or `h:mm:ss` past an hour). Click it for its menu.

| State | Menu bar shows | Menu |
|---|---|---|
| Recording | ● and the running time | **Pause Recording**, **Stop Recording** |
| Paused | ❚❚ and the time, held still | **Resume Recording**, **Stop Recording** |

While the recording records shortcuts, a keyboard mark **⌨︎** follows the ● or ❚❚, in the menu bar's own colour, and the menu starts with a greyed-out **Recording keyboard shortcuts** row and a separa

The item keeps one fixed width, so the other menu-bar items don't shift as the seconds tick. It's a little wider when it shows the keyboard mark. It comes down as soon as the recording stops.

---
### Safe areas

**View ▸ Safe Areas**, or the toolbar's **Safe** checkbox, draws two guide
frames over the canvas, at 90 % and 80 % of its size. They are guides only
and never appear in an export. The app remembers the setting.

---
### Preview Quality

**View ▸ Preview Quality ▸** Full, Half or Quarter draws the preview at a
fraction of the canvas size and scales it back up to fit. It makes heavy
projects play more smoothly. It never changes an export, a saved frame or a
rendered frame. The menu checks the current choice, Full is the default, and
the choice is remembered. The Preview Window (below) shows the same player,
so it draws at the same quality.
